client: I got promoted about six weeks ago, and honestly, I thought I'd feel good about it, but instead I just feel completely overwhelmed all the time. Every day I go into work and I'm convinced that I'm going to mess something up or that people are going to realize I don't actually deserve to be in this role. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is real and it's not going away.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed — a promotion brings real new responsibilities, and those feelings of pressure aren't just in your head. At the same time, I notice there's a thought running underneath all of this, something like *"I don't truly deserve to be here,"* and I'm curious whether that thought is a fact or more of a fear your mind has latched onto. What would you say to a colleague who got promoted and came to you with those exact same doubts?

client: I mean, if a colleague came to me with those doubts, I'd probably tell them that they earned it, that the company saw something in them worth investing in. But it feels so different when it's me saying it to myself — like I'd just be lying to myself or making excuses. I guess I don't fully trust my own reassurance the way I might trust it coming from someone else.
therapist: That gap you've noticed — where you'd trust your own words as wisdom for someone else but dismiss them as excuses when turned inward — is such an important insight, and it tells us something about how harshly you're holding yourself to a different standard. This is actually a really common pattern called the "double standard," where we extend compassion and logic to others but filter it out before it reaches ourselves. I'm wondering, what do you think makes your situation feel like the *exception* to the reassurance that you'd otherwise believe is true?

client: I think part of me feels like... my loneliness is somehow self-inflicted, like I chose to pull away from people, so I don't deserve the same understanding I'd give someone else. If a friend told me they'd been isolating because they were scared of being a burden, I'd tell them that makes complete sense and it doesn't make them a bad person. But when it's me, there's this voice that says I should know better, that I'm old enough to just fix it already. It's like I've convicted myself before even hearing my own case out.
therapist: That phrase — *"convicted yourself before even hearing your own case out"* — is really striking, and it shows a lot of self-awareness about how unfairly your inner voice is treating you. Pulling away when you're scared of being a burden isn't a character flaw; it's actually a very human way of trying to protect the people you care about, even if it ends up hurting you in the process. I'm curious — when did you first start believing that needing others made you a burden?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. I think it goes back pretty far, maybe to when I was a kid and my mom was dealing with her own stuff, depression or stress or whatever it was, and I learned pretty quickly that bringing my problems to her just made things worse for everyone. So somewhere along the way I just... decided that the safest thing was to handle everything alone, and I guess that never really went away.
therapist: What you just described is such an understandable adaptation — a younger version of you learned that staying small and self-sufficient was a way of keeping the peace and protecting someone you loved, and that was genuinely the wisest thing you could do *at the time*. But that old rule — "my needs make things worse for others" — seems like it's still running in the background now, even though you're no longer that child in that situation. I wonder, when you imagine letting someone close to you actually carry a little of this with you, what's the fear that comes up most strongly?

client: I think the fear is that they'll get overwhelmed and pull away, or worse, stay but resent me for it. Like, I've seen it happen before, where I opened up a little and the other person got this look on their face, this kind of... tired look, and I just knew I'd made a mistake. So even hearing you say "let someone carry this with you" sounds nice in theory, but in practice it feels like I'd just be proving that old rule right all over again.
therapist: That moment you described — seeing that tired look and immediately absorbing it as proof that you're too much — sounds like it was really painful, and it makes complete sense that it's stayed with you as evidence for that old rule. But I want to gently ask: is it possible that one person's reaction in one moment became the verdict for every relationship you might ever have, including ones that haven't happened yet? What might it look like to test that rule in a very small, low-stakes way — not a full unburdening, but just the tiniest crack in the door — with someone in your life right now?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows logically that one person's tired look shouldn't define everything. But it wasn't just that one moment — it's like that look confirmed something I'd already suspected about myself for years, something a lot of people had seemed to show me in different ways. As for testing it with someone... I honestly can't think of who that person would even be, because most of the time I feel like I'm on the outside of everyone's life, just kind of hovering there.
therapist: That feeling of hovering just outside everyone's life — close enough to see in but not quite belonging — sounds profoundly lonely, and I want you to know that makes complete sense given how long you've been protecting yourself by staying on the edges. It's hard to build closeness when the very thing you learned to do to stay safe was to not fully enter the room. I'm curious — is there anyone in your life, even someone you feel only a faint connection with, where there's been even one small moment that felt a little warmer or safer than the rest?

client: There's this one coworker, Dani, who sometimes stops by my desk just to chat about nothing in particular — like a TV show or something funny that happened on her commute. It feels okay in those moments, almost normal, but then I immediately start wondering if she's just being polite or if I'm reading too much into it. I guess that's a small thing, but I don't know if it really counts as a real connection.
therapist: Those small, easy moments with Dani — talking about a TV show, sharing something silly — are actually exactly what real connection is made of, and the fact that it feels "almost normal" is worth paying attention to rather than dismissing. I notice your mind quickly moved to "she's probably just being polite," which sounds like that same protective instinct stepping in to keep you from trusting something that might actually be good. What do you think it would feel like to just let those moments with Dani be what they seem, even for a little while, without immediately cross-examining them?

client: Honestly, just hearing you say that made me feel a weird kind of panic, like if I stop questioning it and just... believe it's real, then I'm setting myself up to get hurt way worse when it falls apart. It's easier to keep a little distance, you know, to already have the "I knew it wasn't real" ready in my back pocket. I guess I don't fully trust that those moments mean what they seem to mean, because I've been wrong about that before.
therapist: What you're describing is such a honest and human thing — keeping that "I knew it wasn't real" ready in your pocket is a way of trying to grieve something *before* it hurts you, which makes complete sense when you've been burned by hope before. But I want to reflect something back gently: the distance you maintain to protect yourself from a possible future hurt is also guaranteeing a certain present loneliness, and part of you already knows that cost. I'm wondering — if you could somehow know in advance that those moments with Dani *were* real, what would you actually want to do with that connection?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. If I knew for sure it was real... I think I'd want to actually show up more, like stop holding back this constant low-level commentary in my head that's analyzing everything she says for signs it's falling apart. But even as I say that, there's this immediate voice that goes "yeah, but you'll never actually know that in advance, so what's the point of even imagining it."
therapist: That voice that jumps in to shut down the imagining — "what's the point" — is working really hard to keep you safe, but notice what it just did: it took a moment where you actually knew what you *wanted* and snuffed it out before you could even sit with it. The fact that you could picture showing up more, quieting that commentary, being present with Dani — that's not nothing, that's actually you knowing something true about yourself. What would it mean for you to hold onto that image, even just as a possibility worth protecting, rather than letting that voice have the final word?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to hold onto that image, like there's something in me that responds to it. But then I think about all the times I've shown up with good intentions and still managed to say the wrong thing or get distracted or just... not be enough for Dani. Protecting that image feels almost dangerous, like I'm setting myself up to believe something that history keeps proving wrong.
therapist: I notice something important in what you just said — you moved from imagining a connection that hasn't fully happened yet to already having a history of failing Dani specifically, and I want to gently ask whether that's memory or whether your mind is borrowing from older, more painful stories and placing them onto her. The part of you that responded to that image of showing up more — that's not naivety, that's actually a form of courage trying to find a way through. What if "being enough" isn't something you achieve perfectly in advance, but something that gets built slowly, in exactly the kind of small, ordinary moments you've already been having with her?
